learning_outcomes.text: Correctly and fluently use logarithmic units of power, gain, and attenuation employed in communication systems.
Apply the fundamentals of time and frequency domain analysis to solve problems in communication systems.
Characterize information, as a signal and as a stochastic process, to be transmitted by a communication system, as well as the perturbations that limit the performance of said system.
Describe and distinguish the functional blocks of analog and digital communication systems.
Obtain the fundamental parameters of analog and digital communication systems.
Understand the limitations and performance of different analog and digital modulation systems.
Appropriately evaluate the trade-off between bandwidth and power consumption to achieve a certain quality in a given analog or digital communication system configuration.
Assimilate the fundamentals of decision theory and signal space theory so that they can be applied to solve signal detection problems in digital communication systems.
Understand the main analog and digital modulation techniques to identify the most appropriate technique in a given transmission configuration.
Discuss and evaluate in a group the most appropriate analog and/or digital modulation technique under given operating conditions and restrictions.

Apply knowledge of the different technological alternatives for deploying communication systems to functionally design systems that meet certain pre-imposed requirements and performance specifications.

syllabus_topics: Tools and parameters of utility in digital communication systems. Digital communication system model. Signal and noise representation in signal space. Gram-Schmidt algorithm. Decision criteria. Symbol and bit error probability. Q function and its properties. Error probability bounds. Parameters related to error probability: Eb/N0, C/N, BER, SER. Approximate calculation of Eb/N0 for a generic constellation. Power gain of one modulation versus another. Spectral and power efficiency. Hartley-Shannon formula and Shannon channel capacity limit.

Systems based on amplitude and/or phase modulations under Gaussian channel. Generic block diagram. Conditions for no inter-symbol interference (ISI). Nyquist criterion and consequences. Minimum bandwidth. Raised cosine pulses. Consequences of truncation. Eye diagram. Analysis of amplitude and/or phase modulations (PAM, QAM, PSK, QPSK, OQPSK and DPSK): temporal, spectral and signal space representation, error probability in Gaussian channel, spectral and power efficiency. Example: DVB-S.
Detection of amplitude and/or phase modulated signals in linear channel. Equivalent discrete channel. ML sequence detector. Viterbi algorithm.

Systems based on multicarrier modulations. Introduction and motivation. Conditions for no ISI in Gaussian channel. Continuous and discrete-time systems for Gaussian channel. Parameters of interest and results for Gaussian channel. 1-D and L-D equivalent discrete channel. Continuous and discrete-time systems for linear channel. Spectral representation. Example: DVB-T.
Systems based on frequency modulations. Systems based on FSK and CPFSK. Phase tree. OQPSK representation of MSK modulation. Error probability in Gaussian channel. Spectral and power efficiency.

Systems based on spread spectrum modulations. Direct sequence spread spectrum (DSSS). Generation and detection. Equivalent discrete channel. Frequency hopping spread spectrum (FH). Design of chirp sequences.
assessment_rules: For the ordinary call, the final grade is the sum of the Theory Block (BT) and the Practical Block (BP). The BT has a weight of 60% and consists of a single written theory exam (ET). The BP has a weight of 40% and is obtained from two laboratory projects, where each project (Pi) accounts for 20% of the final grade. Each project Pi is composed of online questionnaires (Ci) with 6% weight, class participation (PCi) with 24% weight, and a practical exam (EPi) with 70% weight, within the project's score. For the extraordinary call, students can choose to take a practical exam (EP) with a 40% weight or keep their BP score. For differentiated evaluation, a single theory exam counts for 100% of the final grade, scaled by 10/6.
